When one organism eats another, energy moves from the consumed organism's body to the
body. After this, the energy often gets
, or converted into other types of energy. For example, when a kelp bass eats kelp, chemical energy from the kelp's body tissues can be transformed into mechanical energy within the bass's body.
Energy that organisms consume and then store in their body tissues as chemical energy has been
to their trophic level. But only about

of the energy present in the body tissues of organisms in one trophic level gets transferred to the next trophic level. Since energy is always conserved, how can there be varying amounts of energy present in different trophic levels?
About

of the chemical energy consumers obtain from eating food is ultimately released to the environment as waste or heat. For example, when a sea otter eats a sea urchin, the otter may only break down about
of the chemical energy stored in the urchin's body. The other half of the chemical energy is in indigestible tissues that pass through the otter's digestive system as waste.

Most of the chemical energy that the otter breaks down is used for cellular respiration and other functions, such as digestion and movement, which release heat as a byproduct. The little energy that remains, about
of what was originally consumed, is stored in the otter's body tissues as it grows. This energy is available to be transferred to the next trophic level when the otter is eaten.

explanationText.text: Phytoplankton are producers, so they occupy the first trophic level. Zooplankton are primary consumers, so they occupy the second trophic level. When the zooplankton eat the phytoplankton, energy flows from the first trophic level to the second trophic level.

content.text: Energy flows in both directions between the kelp and the sea urchin.

explanationText.text: The arrow pointing from the kelp to the sea urchin shows that energy flows in one direction from the consumed organism to its consumer, not in both directions.

explanationText.text: In this food web, two producers make up the first trophic level, four primary consumers make up the second trophic level, four secondary consumers make up the third trophic level, and two tertiary consumers make up the fourth trophic level. There are also two decomposers that occupy multiple trophic levels.

content.text: Each trophic level in this food web is made up of producers and consumers.

explanationText.text: Producers make up the first trophic level of all ecosystems. Consumers make up the second and higher trophic levels. Producers and consumers never make up the same trophic level.

contents.text: Organisms store energy in the chemical bonds of the matter that makes up their body tissues. This chemical energy moves through an ecosystem as organisms in different trophic levels consume each other. Energy always flows in one direction: from a consumed organism to its consumer. So each consumer depends on organisms in lower trophic levels for its energy.

content.text: The trophic levels in this food web contain varying numbers of organisms.

explanationText.text: In this food web, two producers make up the first trophic level, four primary consumers make up the second trophic level, four secondary consumers make up the third trophic level, and two tertiary consumers make up the fourth trophic level. There are also two decomposers that occupy multiple trophic levels.

content.text: When the plainfin midshipman eats the zooplankton, energy flows from the second trophic level to the third trophic level.

explanationText.text: Zooplankton are primary consumers, so they occupy the second trophic level. The plainfin midshipman is a secondary consumer, so it occupies the third trophic level. When the plainfin midshipman eats the zooplankton, energy flows from the second trophic level to the third trophic level.

of the chemical energy consumers obtain from eating food is ultimately released to the environment as waste or heat. For example, when a sea otter eats a sea urchin, the otter may only break down about
of the chemical energy stored in the urchin's body. The other half of the chemical energy is in indigestible tissues that pass through the otter's digestive system as waste.

Most of the chemical energy that the otter breaks down is used for cellular respiration and other functions, such as digestion and movement, which release heat as a byproduct. The little energy that remains, about

contents.text: The fast processes of the carbon cycle are biological, meaning they move carbon to, from, or within the biosphere. Up to 100 billion metric tons of carbon move through the fast processes of the carbon cycle each year!

staticItems.text: Carbon moves from the atmosphere to the biosphere as plants and algae use carbon dioxide gas to make carbon-based molecules, such as carbohydrates.
Carbon moves within the biosphere as animals eat other organisms. They take in and break down carbon-based molecules, and they use the products to generate energy and make new carbon-based molecules.
Carbon moves from the biosphere to the atmosphere as plants and animals break down carbon-based molecules for energy and release carbon dioxide gas.
Carbon moves from the biosphere to the geosphere and atmosphere as fungi and bacteria break down carbon-based molecules in dead organisms.

mainText.text: While the fast processes of the carbon cycle are biological and mainly involve the biosphere, the slow processes of the carbon cycle are primarily geological and involve interactions between the geosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere, with limited biosphere involvement. Each year, up to 100 million metric tons of carbon moves between rocks, soils, bodies of water, and the air via chemical reactions and geological activity. This is less than 1% of the amount of carbon that moves through the biological processes of the carbon cycle annually.

contents.text: Which equation can be used to calculate population growth?

Population growth can be calculated by subtracting the number of individuals that are removed from a population from the number of individuals that are added to the population. Birth and immigration add individuals to the population, while death and emigration remove individuals from the population.
By tracking births, deaths, immigrants, and emigrants, scientists can measure population growth.

Imagine a population of 11 chickens (1 rooster and 10 hens) living on a farm. Over the course of one month, 20 new chicks were born into the flock, 3 of which died. The farmer added 1 new hen to the flock. What was the population growth over this month-long period?

Individuals rarely emigrate from their colony, and colonies rarely receive new immigrants.

is the change in the total number of individuals in a population over some period of time. If more individuals join a population than leave it, then population growth is positive. If more individuals leave a population than join it, then population growth is negative. Individuals join a population by being born or by immigrating from another population. Individuals leave a population by dying or by emigrating to another population.

contents.text: Which equation can be used to calculate population growth?

Population growth can be calculated by subtracting the number of individuals that are removed from a population from the number of individuals that are added to the population. Birth and immigration add individuals to the population, while death and emigration remove individuals from the population.
By tracking births, deaths, immigrants, and emigrants, scientists can measure population growth.

Imagine a population of 11 chickens (1 rooster and 10 hens) living on a farm. Over the course of one month, 20 new chicks were born into the flock, 3 of which died. The farmer added 1 new hen to the flock. What was the population growth over this month-long period?

mainText.text: The naked mole rat is a mammal that lives in underground colonies in eastern Africa. Colonies typically consist of a single reproductive queen, a few reproductive males, and their offspring. The queen can have a litter of pups every three months. Individuals rarely emigrate from their colony, and colonies rarely receive new immigrants.

contents.text: When an environment has more space and resources than a population needs, the population's birth rate may be much higher than its death rate; as a result, the population can grow rapidly. But as the population size approaches the environment's carrying capacity, the environment has less space and fewer resources available for additional individuals, so population growth slows down. This slowed growth may be the result of decreased birth or immigration rates or increased death or emigration rates.

lessons.name: Factors affecting Yellowstone bison population dynamics

contents.text: Bison once roamed across most of North America. The few million bison living east of the Mississippi River were wiped out by 1832 due to hunting and habitat loss, but tens of millions of bison in vast herds still populated the Great Plains between the Rocky Mountains and the Mississippi River. However, beginning around 1870, bison were actively hunted to the brink of extinction. By the end of the 1890s, only a few hundred bison remained, mostly in captive herds. The last wild plains bison herd, numbering about 30 individuals, survived in a remote mountainous region within central Yellowstone National Park.

item.text: In 1902, park managers purchased 21 bison from private herds to establish a second population in the northern region of Yellowstone National Park. Both herds were protected from poachers, and by 1931, there were over 1,300 total bison in the park.

pieces.text: Yellowstone National Park managers' initial goal for the bison population was to protect and restore it. By 1931, there were over 1,300 total bison in the park, mostly in the northern herd. In 1932, a study estimated the northern range's carrying capacity for bison to be only 1,000 individuals. —removing or killing—"excess" bison. By 1966, the Yellowstone bison population had been reduced to fewer than 400 total individuals. Park managers then decided to stop culling bison and let environmental conditions regulate population size instead.

contents.text: Bison once roamed across most of North America. The few million bison living east of the Mississippi River were wiped out by 1832 due to hunting and habitat loss, but tens of millions of bison in vast herds still populated the Great Plains between the Rocky Mountains and the Mississippi River. However, beginning around 1870, bison were actively hunted to the brink of extinction. By the end of the 1890s, only a few hundred bison remained, mostly in captive herds. The last wild plains bison herd, numbering about 30 individuals, survived in a remote mountainous region within central Yellowstone National Park.

item.text: In 1902, park managers purchased 21 bison from private herds to establish a second population in the northern region of Yellowstone National Park. Both herds were protected from poachers, and by 1931, there were over 1,300 total bison in the park.

pieces.text: Ecosystems consist of communities of organisms that interact with each other and their environment. A stable ecosystem tends to maintain a relatively constant variety and number of species. But disruptions can change an ecosystem. After a minor disturbance, like a storm, a stable ecosystem returns quickly to its former state. But after an extreme disturbance, like a volcanic eruption, an ecosystem may be stripped of critical resources, vegetation, and even soil, resulting in a completely new ecosystem.

is the process by which the types of species in a biological community change over time, especially after disruptive events. During succession, as different species come in, an ecosystem progresses through several stages before settling into a stable community. This process can take tens to thousands of years, and the new community might be much different from the original one.

pieces.text: The chaparral of southern California is a dense, woody, evergreen shrubland covering vast areas of hills and mountains. This ecosystem is highly susceptible to fire, which is a frequent natural disturbance due to dense vegetation and hot, dry summers. Fires often reduce the plant cover to ashes, but chaparral plants are adapted to these disturbances. Some species have seeds that only germinate after fire, and many species can resprout from roots or burned stumps.

textContent.text: During the first or second rainy season after a fire, seedlings of small shrubs like black sage and woody shrubs like manzanita can grow on the newly opened land. Shrubs that resprout from underground roots or surviving stumps, such as chamise and scrub oak, quickly grow new shoots. Within 10 to 20 years, scrub oak becomes dominant, and sun-loving shrubs are replaced by shade-tolerant honeysuckle, poison oak, and gooseberry. Chamise is eventually shaded out by larger scrub oaks, becoming less prevalent in areas that have not burned in over 30 years. At this point, the new plant community closely resembles the pre-fire climax community.

title.text: Coille Ruigh na Cuileige

pieces.text: The Caledonian Forest once covered nearly 20% of Scotland, including much of the Highlands. By the 1950s, deforestation for timber and agriculture reduced the forest to only 1% of its original extent, fragmented into many small patches. Wolves in Scotland had been hunted to extinction in the 1740s, so the red deer population in this area exploded. This led to overgrazing—whenever tree seeds sprouted, red deer ate the seedlings, preventing forest regeneration.

textContent.text: In 1990, conservation biologists began building fences around some of the Caledonian Forest patches to keep out deer. Within a few years, heather shrubs covered much of the former grassland inside the exclosures, and birch and Scots pine seedlings began to grow. By 2015, many of these new trees had grown taller than some of the old dead trees in the area. Rowan and holly trees were also growing, and bird and insect biodiversity had increased as well. It is thought that oak and hazel trees will eventually replace birch trees in the climax community.

title.text: Rakata

pieces.text: The 1883 eruption of Krakatau, a volcanic island in Indonesia, was one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in recorded history. The explosion destroyed over 70% of the original island; today, the remnant island is known as Rakata. The event wiped out all plant and animal life on the island, leaving only a barren landscape covered in volcanic ash, lava, and pumice.

textContent.text: Within three years, pioneer species like cyanobacteria covered much of the ash and rock, and wind-blown spores brought ferns from neighboring islands. Over the following decade, seeds from nearby Sumatra and Java were brought in by wind, ocean currents, and bird droppings. Fifteen years after the eruption, dense grassland had largely replaced the ferns, and insects, birds, and small reptiles had arrived on the island. By 1933, tall trees like figs and neonauclea had formed a dense forest canopy inhabited by monitor lizards, snakes, and bats. Today, the dominant species on the island are still tropical evergreen trees. Based on the vegetation of nearby islands, it is thought that the climax community may eventually be a seasonal monsoon forest including some deciduous species.

title.text: Rhizophora-forest

pieces.text: Brazil's coastline is home to extensive forests of red, black, and white mangrove trees. Red mangroves are poor seed dispersers, so seedlings typically grow under their parent trees. Black and white mangrove seedlings are often dispersed by tides. In 1991, farmers near Brazil's northern coast cleared part of a red mangrove forest along a tidal riverbank to grow rice. After about five years, they abandoned the fields due to persistent weeds.

textContent.text: After the final rice harvest, sedges, joyweed, Bermuda grass, and some white mangrove seedlings were the first species to grow in the fields. Within a year, black mangrove seedlings appeared. Within four years, young white and black mangrove trees, along with some shrubs and red mangrove seedlings, had replaced nearly all the original plants. By the sixth year, many fast-growing black mangroves had become large trees, but because they are shade-intolerant, young saplings were unable to mature. By the ninth year, many white mangroves and some red mangroves had also grown into large trees, but black mangrove saplings continued to be shaded out, and no new red mangrove seedlings had dispersed into the area. Because red mangroves largely failed to recolonize the area, and new black mangrove trees couldn't grow, white mangroves dominate the area today.

title.text: Marine outwash plain of glacier Ampère

pieces.text: About 1,500 miles north of Antarctica, the Kerguelen Islands consist of nearly 300 islets surrounding one large island, Grande Terre. Much of Grande Terre is covered by glaciers. The Ampère Glacier near the island's southern end has been receding for over 200 years, leaving behind completely barren sediment.

textContent.text: The plants closest to the glacier's edge are the pioneer species able to live on the silt exposed by the glacier's retreat—a few blades of grass began growing within a year. Where the glacier had retreated 30 years previously, about 1% of the ground is covered by plants, including a few grasses and some flowering plants growing in moss-like cushions. Farther from the glacier's edge, where the ground has been exposed for 115 years and nutrient-rich silt has settled deeper into the ground between pebbles, shallow-rooted grass and cushion plant species have been almost entirely replaced by deeper-rooted species. Farthest away from the glacier, where pebbles have been exposed for over 200 years, still only 4% of the ground is covered by plants, mostly a deep-rooted cushion plant.

pieces.text: Neotoma Valley in the Hocking Hills of Ohio was historically covered by a deciduous forest containing primarily chestnut oak. Additionally, the forest included black oak, red maple, and sourwood, with an understory of blueberry, greenbrier, and mountain laurel. In the early 20th century, large areas of Neotoma Valley were cleared and converted to pastures and corn fields, but this farmland was abandoned around 1920.

textContent.text: For the first few years after the fields were abandoned, grasses and small flowering plants dominated in the absence of trees. After 20 years, the area was populated with large numbers of saplings and shrubs—including aspen, chestnut oak, white oak, pine, sassafras, and sumac—but only a few medium-sized trees. Over the next 25 years, the area developed into a young mixed oak forest. Sumac completely died off, aspen saplings grew into medium-sized trees but died before reaching their full height, and sassafras and pine significantly decreased in abundance. Black and scarlet oaks became codominant with chestnut oak, while only a few white oaks remained. Due to an abundance of chestnut oak saplings and relatively few saplings of other species, scientists believe that the eventual climax community will be dominated by chestnut oak.

pieces.text: In 1988, wildfires swept across much of Yellowstone National Park during the largest fire event in the park's history. Fueled by drought and wind, the fires burned an area of nearly 800,000 acres. About 40% of this area was burned by severe crown fires, which destroyed all the trees and understory plants in their path. Despite the destruction, many seeds beneath the soil remained unharmed.

textContent.text: Within weeks following the fire, many plants began to grow back, boosted by ash nutrients and sunlight. Lodgepole pine trees sprouted from fire-released seeds, and fireweed and aspen shrubs sprouted from underground roots. Thousands of aspen seedlings also appeared in 1989. In 1991, fireweed peaked, forming thick patches of waist-high flowers, before declining as it was outcompeted by other plants. After seven years, aspen shrubs had regrown to their pre-burn size, and many aspen seedlings were still growing. By 2010, most aspen saplings in lodgepole pine areas had been suppressed or killed by browsing elk. If undisturbed for a few more decades, lodgepole pines will form a dense canopy, shading out aspen. Over centuries, shade-tolerant spruce and fir will replace the pines, eventually leading to a stable spruce-fir forest unless another major disturbance occurs.

title.text: Wildflowers and Mount St Helens

pieces.text: In the spring of 1980, Mount St. Helens volcano in Washington state erupted in what would prove to be the worst volcanic disaster in United States history. The explosion blew a cloud of ash 15 miles in the air, left the mountain a quarter-mile shorter, and destroyed the surrounding landscape. Many areas around Mount St. Helens were left totally devoid of plant and animal life, having been scoured by hot rocks and ash.

textContent.text: The Pumice Plain was one area sterilized by hot gas, ash, and volcanic rock. The ash that covered the area contained very few nutrients, making survival difficult for pioneer species. However, prairie lupine—a wildflower able to cycle nitrogen into the barren, ashy soil—was found growing on the Pumice Plain two years after the eruption. It also trapped wind-blown organic debris and attracted insects. Other small flowers with lightweight seeds, like pearly everlasting, were carried to the area by wind. Over the next 30 years, larger plants like Pacific silver fir, mountain hemlock, and red alder trees became established. Scientists predict the area will eventually be dominated by some of these trees, although this process will likely take several hundred years.

pieces.text: Brazil's coastline is home to extensive forests of red, black, and white mangrove trees. Red mangroves are poor seed dispersers, so seedlings typically grow under their parent trees. Black and white mangrove seedlings are often dispersed by tides. In 1991, farmers near Brazil's northern coast cleared part of a red mangrove forest along a tidal riverbank to grow rice. After about five years, they abandoned the fields due to persistent weeds.

textContent.text: After the final rice harvest, sedges, joyweed, Bermuda grass, and some white mangrove seedlings were the first species to grow in the fields. Within a year, black mangrove seedlings appeared. Within four years, young white and black mangrove trees, along with some shrubs and red mangrove seedlings, had replaced nearly all the original plants. By the sixth year, many fast-growing black mangroves had become large trees, but because they are shade-intolerant, young saplings were unable to mature. By the ninth year, many white mangroves and some red mangroves had also grown into large trees, but black mangrove saplings continued to be shaded out, and no new red mangrove seedlings had dispersed into the area. Because red mangroves largely failed to recolonize the area, and new black mangrove trees couldn't grow, white mangroves dominate the area today.

title.text: Marine outwash plain of glacier Ampère

pieces.text: About 1,500 miles north of Antarctica, the Kerguelen Islands consist of nearly 300 islets surrounding one large island, Grande Terre. Much of Grande Terre is covered by glaciers. The Ampère Glacier near the island's southern end has been receding for over 200 years, leaving behind completely barren sediment.

textContent.text: The plants closest to the glacier's edge are the pioneer species able to live on the silt exposed by the glacier's retreat—a few blades of grass began growing within a year. Where the glacier had retreated 30 years previously, about 1% of the ground is covered by plants, including a few grasses and some flowering plants growing in moss-like cushions. Farther from the glacier's edge, where the ground has been exposed for 115 years and nutrient-rich silt has settled deeper into the ground between pebbles, shallow-rooted grass and cushion plant species have been almost entirely replaced by deeper-rooted species. Farthest away from the glacier, where pebbles have been exposed for over 200 years, still only 4% of the ground is covered by plants, mostly a deep-rooted cushion plant.

title.text: Coille Ruigh na Cuileige

pieces.text: The Caledonian Forest once covered nearly 20% of Scotland, including much of the Highlands. By the 1950s, deforestation for timber and agriculture reduced the forest to only 1% of its original extent, fragmented into many small patches. Wolves in Scotland had been hunted to extinction in the 1740s, so the red deer population in this area exploded. This led to overgrazing—whenever tree seeds sprouted, red deer ate the seedlings, preventing forest regeneration.

textContent.text: In 1990, conservation biologists began building fences around some of the Caledonian Forest patches to keep out deer. Within a few years, heather shrubs covered much of the former grassland inside the exclosures, and birch and Scots pine seedlings began to grow. By 2015, many of these new trees had grown taller than some of the old dead trees in the area. Rowan and holly trees were also growing, and bird and insect biodiversity had increased as well. It is thought that oak and hazel trees will eventually replace birch trees in the climax community.

title.text: Red fox hidden in grass watches a burning wildfire in Everglades, Florida USA

pieces.text: Fires have played an important role in shaping many ecosystems, including the Florida Everglades. Fires help maintain sawgrass marshes by returning nutrients to the soil and controlling the growth of shrubs and trees. Natural fires are periodically started by lightning, but since the 1950s, they have been reduced in the Everglades. Near human developments, roads and canals keep fires from spreading, and firefighters quickly extinguish them. As a result, some areas that once experienced regular fires have not burned in nearly 75 years.

textContent.text: Although fire in a sawgrass marsh kills small woody plants, sawgrass grows back quickly from underground roots, especially with the extra nutrients released into the soil. Within 10 years after a fire, water-tolerant shrubs like willow invade the area. After 20 years without fire, marshes transition to swamps—dense thickets of shrubs replace the sawgrass, and cypress trees begin to grow. After 30 years without fire, cypress shades out most shrubs, and after 50 years, hardwoods such as ash, red maple, and pond apple also grow. Without another fire, these trees will eventually form a dense mixed cypress-hardwood swamp forest.

lessons.name: How can group behavior affect survival? Identify evidence to support a claim

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in Japanese macaques.

alternativeText.text: macaques

textContent.text: Japanese macaques, also called snow monkeys, inhabit a variety of forest ecosystems in Japan. Japanese macaques are omnivores that feed on a wide variety of plant material, insects, and fish. They live in groups called troops led by an alpha male. Troops have a female-bonded social structure: Females remain in the same troop their entire lives, while males leave their natal troop to find a new troop once they mature.

Social grooming, a behavior where Japanese macaques clean the fur of other macaques, is a common practice among troop members. Social grooming not only strengthens social bonds among macaques, it also reduces the number of parasites in their fur. Macaques often remove harmful pests, like disease-spreading ticks and lice, from the fur of their troop mates as they groom. Troop members are also known to take care of each other by sharing food and sounding an alarm call to warn other macaques when they spot a predator.

Japanese macaques live further north than any other nonhuman primate. Several physical and behavioral adaptations help them survive in the extreme cold. For example, their yellowish-brown fur grows thicker in the winter to help them keep warm. Japanese macaques have also been known to enter hot springs to warm up!

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in American white pelicans.

alternativeText.text: many pelicans swimming together

textContent.text: American white pelicans are one of the largest birds in North America. Unlike other species of pelicans that dive from the air to catch fish, American white pelicans feed in shallow bodies of water by swimming on the water's surface and dipping their bill in the water to scoop up fish. They often collaborate to forage for fish more efficiently. By swimming together as a group, the pelicans can drive entire schools of fish into shallower water where they can be easily scooped up and eaten.

American white pelicans have long bills and a stretchy, featherless pouch near their throat, called a gular pouch. This pouch is a flap of skin that is used to hold fish—it has up to three times the capacity of the pelican's stomach! A pelican catches fish by scooping up fish and water into its gular pouch. The pelican then closes its bill, presses the pouch against its chest to push the water out, and swallows the fish whole. American white pelicans can also use their gular pouches for temperature control. Because the pouches contain many blood vessels, pelicans will face away from the sun and shake their gular pouches to release heat and cool down.

title.text: The colony of American cliff swallows building their nests on the cliff edge

alternativeText.text: several cliff swallows

textContent.text: Cliff swallows are small birds that live in North America during their breeding season and migrate into Central and South America for the winter. These fast fliers mainly feed on flying insects. They build their nests on mountain cliffs, canyon walls, and even man-made structures, like buildings and bridges. Cliff swallows are social birds that form large colonies. Members of a colony interact in many ways—both positive and negative. Some females engage in brood parasitism, where a female lays her eggs in another swallow's nest. She can trick that nest's owner into caring for her chicks!

Most interactions within a colony are mutually beneficial for the cliff swallows. Members share information about food locations, clean each other, and even play together. They also look out for predators that can attack the nesting site, such as falcons or hawks. When a cliff swallow spots a threat, it makes a purr call. This distinctive sound prompts the other swallows in the colony to escape in a mass flock. Some predators have become so familiar with the purr call that its sound will cause them to forfeit their attack and leave.

Living in colonies increases the chances that cliff swallows will be able to evade a predator attack.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in European starlings.

alternativeText.text: many birds flying together

textContent.text: European starlings are black songbirds that can imitate the calls of many other bird species. In the summer, they are dark and glossy, but during the winter, they are covered in white spots. They are known for flying in mesmerizing flocks of thousands of birds before they descend to roost for the evening. These large synchronized groups, called murmurations, look like swirling clouds in the sky. Scientists believe one benefit of murmurations is protection from predators. The whirling movement makes it harder for a falcon or hawk to track a single bird. The presence of so many birds in one place also makes it more likely that predators will be spotted by the flock and lessens the odds that an individual bird will become prey should a predator attack.

As their name suggests, European starlings are native to Europe, but there is also a large population in North America. The North American birds are all closely related because they are all descendants of a small group of birds that were released in New York in the late 1800s by a group of Shakespeare enthusiasts who wanted America to have all the birds that Shakespeare ever mentioned. Today, European starlings are so numerous from Alaska to Mexico that many people consider them pests.

alternativeText.text: several spiders on a web

textContent.text: Although most spiders are solitary, some species tend to live together in colonies that share communal webs. One species, the African social spider, forms colonies that range in size from just a few individuals to hundreds of spiders. Colony members are mainly female, as the males have much shorter lifespans. Most of the females in the colony do not reproduce, but they all help care for offspring. Some even sacrifice themselves as food for the young.

African social spiders also cooperate in building and maintaining a large shared web. This requires less work and silk from each spider than would be needed for individual webs. Maintaining a large shared web also allows the African social spiders to catch larger prey than they could alone. Some colonies have webs that are large enough to capture birds and bats! When large prey gets stuck in the communal web, many social spiders then inject the prey with their digestive juices. This breaks the prey down into a liquid that the whole colony can share.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in Canada geese.

alternativeText.text: many geese flying together

textContent.text: Canada geese, known for their signature honking calls, were almost hunted to extinction in the early 1900s. Conservation efforts have been so effective that their populations have made a major comeback. Now, they are commonly seen (and heard!) across most of North America. Many Canada geese migrate north into Canada in the spring to capitalize on abundant food and nesting locations and then migrate as far south as Mexico for the winter as the food supply decreases in the north. While migrating, a group of 30 to 100 Canada geese flies in a characteristic V-shaped formation.

As a goose flies, it disrupts the air in a way that creates an updraft on both sides. Each goose in the V-shaped formation flies slightly above and to the side of the goose in front of it to catch a free lift on the upward-moving current of air. This helps geese conserve energy during their lengthy migrations. It may also aid communication and coordination within the group.

A V-shaped formation helps each goose conserve energy, except for one: the leader at the front of the V. Canada geese continually shift positions to take turns in the front, falling back as they grow tired. So, the group can fly for a long time before stopping to rest. Geese aren't the only ones that use this flight formation—fighter pilots often fly in a V to increase fuel efficiency and facilitate communication.

textContent.text: Brandt's voles are small, brown rodents that live in shrublands and grasslands in Russia, Mongolia, and northern China. Brandt's voles live in family groups and have evolved many strategies for surviving the bitterly cold winters in their habitat. For example, they spend the winter in complex burrows underground and block the exits to conserve heat. During this time, they live off of stored food to avoid venturing out into the cold. Family members also huddle together, a behavior that allows them to have lower resting metabolic rates and thus conserve more heat, burn fewer calories, and consume less of the stored food than voles that do not huddle.

During the summer, Brandt's voles are much more active above ground. They live in simpler burrows and fiercely defend their territory. When they spot danger, they make alarm calls to warn others. During the breeding season, females can give birth to four litters of about seven young. As the breeding season ends, Brandt's voles store food to prepare for another winter underground.

alternativeText.text: several dholes

textContent.text: Dholes (pronounced "doles") are wild dogs found in eastern and southern Asia. Also called red dogs or whistling dogs, dholes use vocalizations to communicate. Dholes will scream, whistle, mew like a cat, and even cluck like a chicken!

Dholes are very social, forming packs of up to 12 members. Packs are led by one dominant mating pair. Dholes display cooperative breeding, in which the entire pack helps to care for and feed the dominant pair's offspring. Individual dholes forage for small food items like wild berries, insects, and lizards, but dholes also hunt larger animals as a group.

Dhole packs sometimes join together to hunt in super packs of around 30 members. Super packs can take down larger mammals than dholes could alone or in their smaller packs. After a successful hunt, the dholes share their prey. After eating their fill, dholes will eat the extra meat whole to bring back and regurgitate for the nursing dominant female and her pups.

textContent.text: Japanese macaques, also called snow monkeys, inhabit a variety of forest ecosystems in Japan. Japanese macaques are omnivores that feed on a wide variety of plant material, insects, and fish. They live in groups called troops led by an alpha male. Troops have a female-bonded social structure: Females remain in the same troop their entire lives, while males leave their natal troop to find a new troop once they mature.

Social grooming, a behavior where Japanese macaques clean the fur of other macaques, is a common practice among troop members. Social grooming not only strengthens social bonds among macaques, it also reduces the number of parasites in their fur. Macaques often remove harmful pests, like disease-spreading ticks and lice, from the fur of their troop mates as they groom. Troop members are also known to take care of each other by sharing food and sounding an alarm call to warn other macaques when they spot a predator.

Japanese macaques live further north than any other nonhuman primate. Several physical and behavioral adaptations help them survive in the extreme cold. For example, their yellowish-brown fur grows thicker in the winter to help them keep warm. Japanese macaques have also been known to enter hot springs to warm up!

alternativeText.text: several birds in a tree

textContent.text: The aptly named Florida scrub-jay is the only species of bird that lives exclusively in the state of Florida, in scrub habitats in the central part of the state. These blue-and-gray songbirds are omnivores that feed on a variety of seeds, insects, reptiles, and rodents. Florida scrub-jays are also cooperative breeders; before they obtain a territory of their own, these birds often stay with their parents and help raise new offspring. These non-breeding helpers handle tasks such as feeding their fledgling siblings and defending the nesting territory.

Members of a Florida scrub-jay family unit take turns watching for predators, such as hawks and snakes, while the rest of the birds search for food. When the lookout spots a predator, it makes an alarm call, prompting the other family members to either take cover or attack the predator. Studies show that fledglings are less likely to be preyed upon and more likely to become independent juveniles when they are raised in family units with non-breeding helpers than when they are raised by their parents alone.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in European starlings.

alternativeText.text: many birds flying together

textContent.text: European starlings are black songbirds that can imitate the calls of many other bird species. In the summer, they are dark and glossy, but during the winter, they are covered in white spots. They are known for flying in mesmerizing flocks of thousands of birds before they descend to roost for the evening. These large synchronized groups, called murmurations, look like swirling clouds in the sky. Scientists believe one benefit of murmurations is protection from predators. The whirling movement makes it harder for a falcon or hawk to track a single bird. The presence of so many birds in one place also makes it more likely that predators will be spotted by the flock and lessens the odds that an individual bird will become prey should a predator attack.

As their name suggests, European starlings are native to Europe, but there is also a large population in North America. The North American birds are all closely related because they are all descendants of a small group of birds that were released in New York in the late 1800s by a group of Shakespeare enthusiasts who wanted America to have all the birds that Shakespeare ever mentioned. Today, European starlings are so numerous from Alaska to Mexico that many people consider them pests.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in banded mongooses.

alternativeText.text: several mongooses

textContent.text: Banded mongooses are small carnivores that are native to the open grasslands of Africa. Mongooses have the ability to fight and kill snakes, including venomous species such as cobras. In fact, many species of mongooses have a genetic mutation that makes them resistant to snake venom!

While most mongooses live alone, banded mongooses live in colonies with numbers reaching up to 40 per group. Females in a colony usually give birth at the same time. After a few weeks, the group of pups emerges from the den, and each pup spends at least three days bonding with an unrelated adult mongoose that becomes its escort. The escort feeds, grooms, and plays with its bonded pup for up to 13 weeks, until the pup becomes independent. This behavior relieves the parents from having to care for a whole litter themselves, and also frees the pups from having to compete with their siblings for food since they each have their own escort.

textContent.text: Dholes (pronounced "doles") are wild dogs found in eastern and southern Asia. Also called red dogs or whistling dogs, dholes use vocalizations to communicate. Dholes will scream, whistle, mew like a cat, and even cluck like a chicken!

Dholes are very social, forming packs of up to 12 members. Packs are led by one dominant mating pair. Dholes display cooperative breeding, in which the entire pack helps to care for and feed the dominant pair's offspring. Individual dholes forage for small food items like wild berries, insects, and lizards, but dholes also hunt larger animals as a group.

Dhole packs sometimes join together to hunt in super packs of around 30 members. Super packs can take down larger mammals than dholes could alone or in their smaller packs. After a successful hunt, the dholes share their prey. After eating their fill, dholes will eat the extra meat whole to bring back and regurgitate for the nursing dominant female and her pups.

alternativeText.text: a spiny lobster

textContent.text: Spiny lobsters are native to the ocean floor of south Florida and the Caribbean. They can grow up to 15 pounds and are often harvested for their tail meat. Spiny lobsters live up to their name: They have two horn-like spines over their eyes, long spiny antennae, and spines on their bodies that provide protection from predators. They typically reproduce in shallow reefs from April through October, then congregate and form single-file lines to migrate into deeper waters for the winter. By walking antennae-to-tail, the lobsters sustain less drag per individual in a group than they would by migrating alone.

Spiny lobsters are nocturnal, emerging at night to feed on mollusks, crabs, and urchins. They can detect chemical cues released in the urine of other lobsters to locate safe shelters where they can hide from predators like groupers, sharks, turtles, and snappers. Spiny lobsters can use these same chemical cues to detect and avoid unhealthy lobsters suffering from infection.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in European starlings.

alternativeText.text: many birds flying together

textContent.text: European starlings are black songbirds that can imitate the calls of many other bird species. In the summer, they are dark and glossy, but during the winter, they are covered in white spots. They are known for flying in mesmerizing flocks of thousands of birds before they descend to roost for the evening. These large synchronized groups, called murmurations, look like swirling clouds in the sky. Scientists believe one benefit of murmurations is protection from predators. The whirling movement makes it harder for a falcon or hawk to track a single bird. The presence of so many birds in one place also makes it more likely that predators will be spotted by the flock and lessens the odds that an individual bird will become prey should a predator attack.

As their name suggests, European starlings are native to Europe, but there is also a large population in North America. The North American birds are all closely related because they are all descendants of a small group of birds that were released in New York in the late 1800s by a group of Shakespeare enthusiasts who wanted America to have all the birds that Shakespeare ever mentioned. Today, European starlings are so numerous from Alaska to Mexico that many people consider them pests.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in Japanese macaques.

alternativeText.text: macaques

textContent.text: Japanese macaques, also called snow monkeys, inhabit a variety of forest ecosystems in Japan. Japanese macaques are omnivores that feed on a wide variety of plant material, insects, and fish. They live in groups called troops led by an alpha male. Troops have a female-bonded social structure: Females remain in the same troop their entire lives, while males leave their natal troop to find a new troop once they mature.

Social grooming, a behavior where Japanese macaques clean the fur of other macaques, is a common practice among troop members. Social grooming not only strengthens social bonds among macaques, it also reduces the number of parasites in their fur. Macaques often remove harmful pests, like disease-spreading ticks and lice, from the fur of their troop mates as they groom. Troop members are also known to take care of each other by sharing food and sounding an alarm call to warn other macaques when they spot a predator.

Japanese macaques live further north than any other nonhuman primate. Several physical and behavioral adaptations help them survive in the extreme cold. For example, their yellowish-brown fur grows thicker in the winter to help them keep warm. Japanese macaques have also been known to enter hot springs to warm up!

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in Florida scrub-jays.

alternativeText.text: several birds in a tree

textContent.text: The aptly named Florida scrub-jay is the only species of bird that lives exclusively in the state of Florida, in scrub habitats in the central part of the state. These blue-and-gray songbirds are omnivores that feed on a variety of seeds, insects, reptiles, and rodents. Florida scrub-jays are also cooperative breeders; before they obtain a territory of their own, these birds often stay with their parents and help raise new offspring. These non-breeding helpers handle tasks such as feeding their fledgling siblings and defending the nesting territory.

Members of a Florida scrub-jay family unit take turns watching for predators, such as hawks and snakes, while the rest of the birds search for food. When the lookout spots a predator, it makes an alarm call, prompting the other family members to either take cover or attack the predator. Studies show that fledglings are less likely to be preyed upon and more likely to become independent juveniles when they are raised in family units with non-breeding helpers than when they are raised by their parents alone.

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in African social spiders.

alternativeText.text: several spiders on a web

textContent.text: Although most spiders are solitary, some species tend to live together in colonies that share communal webs. One species, the African social spider, forms colonies that range in size from just a few individuals to hundreds of spiders. Colony members are mainly female, as the males have much shorter lifespans. Most of the females in the colony do not reproduce, but they all help care for offspring. Some even sacrifice themselves as food for the young.

African social spiders also cooperate in building and maintaining a large shared web. This requires less work and silk from each spider than would be needed for individual webs. Maintaining a large shared web also allows the African social spiders to catch larger prey than they could alone. Some colonies have webs that are large enough to capture birds and bats! When large prey gets stuck in the communal web, many social spiders then inject the prey with their digestive juices. This breaks the prey down into a liquid that the whole colony can share.

textContent.text: Brandt's voles are small, brown rodents that live in shrublands and grasslands in Russia, Mongolia, and northern China. Brandt's voles live in family groups and have evolved many strategies for surviving the bitterly cold winters in their habitat. For example, they spend the winter in complex burrows underground and block the exits to conserve heat. During this time, they live off of stored food to avoid venturing out into the cold. Family members also huddle together, a behavior that allows them to have lower resting metabolic rates and thus conserve more heat, burn fewer calories, and consume less of the stored food than voles that do not huddle.

During the summer, Brandt's voles are much more active above ground. They live in simpler burrows and fiercely defend their territory. When they spot danger, they make alarm calls to warn others. During the breeding season, females can give birth to four litters of about seven young. As the breeding season ends, Brandt's voles store food to prepare for another winter underground.

alternativeText.text: many birds flying together

textContent.text: European starlings are black songbirds that can imitate the calls of many other bird species. In the summer, they are dark and glossy, but during the winter, they are covered in white spots. They are known for flying in mesmerizing flocks of thousands of birds before they descend to roost for the evening. These large synchronized groups, called murmurations, look like swirling clouds in the sky. Scientists believe one benefit of murmurations is protection from predators. The whirling movement makes it harder for a falcon or hawk to track a single bird. The presence of so many birds in one place also makes it more likely that predators will be spotted by the flock and lessens the odds that an individual bird will become prey should a predator attack.

As their name suggests, European starlings are native to Europe, but there is also a large population in North America. The North American birds are all closely related because they are all descendants of a small group of birds that were released in New York in the late 1800s by a group of Shakespeare enthusiasts who wanted America to have all the birds that Shakespeare ever mentioned. Today, European starlings are so numerous from Alaska to Mexico that many people consider them pests.

alternativeText.text: macaques

textContent.text: Japanese macaques, also called snow monkeys, inhabit a variety of forest ecosystems in Japan. Japanese macaques are omnivores that feed on a wide variety of plant material, insects, and fish. They live in groups called troops led by an alpha male. Troops have a female-bonded social structure: Females remain in the same troop their entire lives, while males leave their natal troop to find a new troop once they mature.

Social grooming, a behavior where Japanese macaques clean the fur of other macaques, is a common practice among troop members. Social grooming not only strengthens social bonds among macaques, it also reduces the number of parasites in their fur. Macaques often remove harmful pests, like disease-spreading ticks and lice, from the fur of their troop mates as they groom. Troop members are also known to take care of each other by sharing food and sounding an alarm call to warn other macaques when they spot a predator.

Japanese macaques live further north than any other nonhuman primate. Several physical and behavioral adaptations help them survive in the extreme cold. For example, their yellowish-brown fur grows thicker in the winter to help them keep warm. Japanese macaques have also been known to enter hot springs to warm up!

contents.text: Read the passage to learn about a group behavior in Canada geese.

alternativeText.text: many geese flying together

textContent.text: Canada geese, known for their signature honking calls, were almost hunted to extinction in the early 1900s. Conservation efforts have been so effective that their populations have made a major comeback. Now, they are commonly seen (and heard!) across most of North America. Many Canada geese migrate north into Canada in the spring to capitalize on abundant food and nesting locations and then migrate as far south as Mexico for the winter as the food supply decreases in the north. While migrating, a group of 30 to 100 Canada geese flies in a characteristic V-shaped formation.

As a goose flies, it disrupts the air in a way that creates an updraft on both sides. Each goose in the V-shaped formation flies slightly above and to the side of the goose in front of it to catch a free lift on the upward-moving current of air. This helps geese conserve energy during their lengthy migrations. It may also aid communication and coordination within the group.

A V-shaped formation helps each goose conserve energy, except for one: the leader at the front of the V. Canada geese continually shift positions to take turns in the front, falling back as they grow tired. So, the group can fly for a long time before stopping to rest. Geese aren't the only ones that use this flight formation—fighter pilots often fly in a V to increase fuel efficiency and facilitate communication.

textContent.text: The aptly named Florida scrub-jay is the only species of bird that lives exclusively in the state of Florida, in scrub habitats in the central part of the state. These blue-and-gray songbirds are omnivores that feed on a variety of seeds, insects, reptiles, and rodents. Florida scrub-jays are also cooperative breeders; before they obtain a territory of their own, these birds often stay with their parents and help raise new offspring. These non-breeding helpers handle tasks such as feeding their fledgling siblings and defending the nesting territory.

Members of a Florida scrub-jay family unit take turns watching for predators, such as hawks and snakes, while the rest of the birds search for food. When the lookout spots a predator, it makes an alarm call, prompting the other family members to either take cover or attack the predator. Studies show that fledglings are less likely to be preyed upon and more likely to become independent juveniles when they are raised in family units with non-breeding helpers than when they are raised by their parents alone.

textContent.text: The aptly named Florida scrub-jay is the only species of bird that lives exclusively in the state of Florida, in scrub habitats in the central part of the state. These blue-and-gray songbirds are omnivores that feed on a variety of seeds, insects, reptiles, and rodents. Florida scrub-jays are also cooperative breeders; before they obtain a territory of their own, these birds often stay with their parents and help raise new offspring. These non-breeding helpers handle tasks such as feeding their fledgling siblings and defending the nesting territory.

Members of a Florida scrub-jay family unit take turns watching for predators, such as hawks and snakes, while the rest of the birds search for food. When the lookout spots a predator, it makes an alarm call, prompting the other family members to either take cover or attack the predator. Studies show that fledglings are less likely to be preyed upon and more likely to become independent juveniles when they are raised in family units with non-breeding helpers than when they are raised by their parents alone.

contents.text: Which claim best describes how a group behavior increases the likelihood of survival for Florida scrub-jays?

choices.text: Defending their territory increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will avoid infection.
Cooperative breeding increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will be protected against hawks and snakes.
Being omnivores increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will eat a wide variety of plants and animals in their habitat.
Making an alarm call increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will live in central Florida.

contents.text: This claim describes how a group behavior increases the likelihood of survival for Florida scrub-jays.

content.text: Cooperative breeding increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will be protected against hawks and snakes.

explanationText.text: Studies show that fledgling Florida scrub-jays are less likely to be killed by predators, like hawks and snakes, and more likely to grow into independent juveniles when they are raised cooperatively in family units with non-breeding helpers than when they are raised by their parents alone.

contents.text: These claims do not describe how a group behavior increases the likelihood of survival for Florida scrub-jays.

content.text: Defending their territory increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will avoid infection.

explanationText.text: Defending their territory from intruders does not increase the likelihood that Florida scrub-jays will avoid infection.

content.text: Being omnivores increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will eat a wide variety of plants and animals in their habitat.

explanationText.text: Being an omnivore is an individual behavior of Florida scrub-jays, not a group behavior.

content.text: Making an alarm call increases the chances that Florida scrub-jays will live in central Florida.

explanationText.text: Making an alarm call alerts other family members to danger. It does not increase the likelihood that Florida scrub-jays will live in central Florida.
